analysis.body:
# Grid Interconnection Snapshot: What It Means for AI Power Demand

Across the five major US grid operators tracked here, 8,378 generation and storage projects totaling 1.33 million megawatts are in various stages of interconnection—a baseline for understanding available power supply growth. ERCOT (Texas) leads with 438,086 MW in 1,778 requests, followed by NYISO (New York) at 319,115 MW and MISO (Midwest) at 299,721 MW. These queues represent planned infrastructure waiting to connect; they are not direct measurements of data center demand, but the fuel mix tells a story: gas represents 184,344 MW across all queues, while storage alone accounts for 326,600 MW, and solar 279,137 MW. The heavy weighting toward storage and gas—fuels that typically scale with sustained load growth—aligns with infrastructure planning for round-the-clock compute demand.

Commercial electricity sales in June 2026 across eight major states totaled 54,798 MWh, with Texas accounting for 15,754 MWh at $8.66 per MWh, the lowest price of the states shown. California's sales of 10,025 MWh carried the highest price at $27.33 per MWh, while Virginia logged 7,771 MWh. These figures proxy data center load since data centers bill mostly in the commercial class, though they do not isolate data center consumption from other commercial users. Texas, Georgia, and Ohio show the largest absolute sales; California and Virginia show the highest per-unit costs. Price spread—from $8.66 in Texas to $27.33 in California—creates geographic incentives that likely influence where new AI infrastructure seeks interconnection slots.

Storage projects in the interconnection queues (326,600 MW total) suggest that grid operators expect sustained demand requiring both renewable and dispatchable backup power. Gas additions (184,344 MW) will likely support baseline load, while the dominance of solar (279,137 MW) and wind (164,966 MW) indicates expectation of peak-shaving and time-shifting rather than sole reliance on either. Watch next for ERCOT and CAISO queue completion rates over the next quarter, as commissioning speed in the highest-cost and lowest-cost regions will signal whether AI load growth is outpacing the planned supply ramp.
